notes.urn:cts:latinLit:tmp1220.tmp1220.opp-lat: Many scanning errors silently corrected (e.g. 'nonestis honorotisque' = honestis honoratisque, 'pndore' = pudore, 'apcibus' = apicibus, 'mediis' in context; 'germirii' read as germini). In I the bracketed variant '[Al., factam pro eo]' is an editorial note and omitted. In II 'mater parentis' is taken as Stratidius' mother. In III 'terni lustri' (fifteen years) may refer to his age; 'Lausia' unidentified with certainty. In VI 'sidera mento' read as 'sidera mente'; 'ante currentem medelam' rendered by the bracketed variant 'praecurrente medela'. In VII the horned face alludes to the Vulgate's 'cornuta' face of Moses (Exod. 34). In X 'nec tamen orationi quoque occurreret' is obscure; 'parvum ... flagitium posteris transiret in luctum' is difficult and possibly corrupt (perhaps 'in lucrum', 'into gain', which suits the context better). In XI 'eulogiis' = blessed bread/blessed gifts.

XII: 'mediis' read as 'inediis' (fasts). XIII: the sentence on the king's breaking up plate is loosely attached; 'quidquid primum habuit' rendered literally. XVI: 'Moglidonensis' unidentified. XVIII: the household name is uncertain in the edition (Nantharicus; the editor queries Nemptodorum/Nanterre); 'Spedotenum' unidentified. XXI: section number printed 'xii.' corrected to XXI. XXII: the last sentence seems to refer to the dead horse being dragged out by the feet; 'qui' is ambiguous.

XXV: 'Iuvem' read as 'novem' (nine); 'si targeret' as 'si tangeret'. XXVI: 'Reali' read as 'sancti' (a Saint's presence); 'hospes' preferred over the variant 'hostis'. XXVII: 'repulsus est' is noted in the edition as standing for 'repulit'. XXX: the closing words of the passage are garbled in the scan; 'culpabilibus' and 'fisco' are assumed. XXXI: the final words 'a I; eniso' are corrupt; 'alienis' (of others) is assumed. XXXII: the widow's name is uncertain, Panitia (variant Pistoficia); 'parentales bestias' is taken as 'related beasts'. XXXV: 'caligas circinasset' is rendered literally ('rounded' his boots); the exact meaning of this colloquial phrase, perhaps trimming or sewing, is unclear. XXXVI: the editor glosses Amoniense as Mosny in Brie and Rotegiacum as Rozoy.

XXXVII: 'thorace pectoris vitali appulsus' is obscure; rendered loosely. XL: 'ex improviso ... salutem suam oculi lacrymabant' read as eyes weeping out the disease; the attendants' remark ('for money') is odd and may be corrupt. XLIV: opening lacks a subject ('Tradidit memoriae'); 'ideos' read as 'fidens'; 'racbena' as 'rachena' (blanket). XLV: 'Baudo Feifa' taken as one name, Baudofeifa; 'Sene Corbiaco' as Senecorbiacum. XLVI: 'lanii' read as 'tantum'. XLVII: 'chrismaria' are vessels or reliquaries for chrism/relics. XLVIII: 'mysteriuen' read as 'mysterium'.

LI: 'Libanins' read as Libanius. LII: 'vincula' read as vinea (vineyard); the edition's note offers 'die Dominico' as a variant for 'die Resurrectionis'. LIII: 'ealcaretur' read as calcaretur; the phrase 'ut nec calcaretur' is awkward and its sense uncertain. LIV: 'res luminis' taken from 'res uminis'; 'specularibus' (windows) taken figuratively of the eyes. LVII: very corrupt passage; 'domui Germani' read as domni Germani; 'praedicti' taken as genitive referring to Germanus; 'qua sorte' rendered 'by some chance'. LX: 'missa revocata' is obscure (the edition flags it); rendered loosely as 'mass said'. LXI: 'saeculum' read as sacculum (bag), 'ampi' as ampli; 'mercedem vitae vel gratiae' uncertain. LXII: 'tormonti' read as tormenti. LXIII: 'per obsidem' (through a hostage/besieger) is obscure. LXIV: 'peregrinula lux oculi' rendered 'wandering light of an eye'; 'natutam' read as naturam.

LXV: 'dissimulabant ... reserare' read as the Jews pretending to be unable to open the chains; the sense is compressed. LXVII: 'trusis' taken as 'to those thrust [in prison]'. LXXI: 'Moverla' may be a name; the variant 'Noverca' would mean 'a certain stepmother'. LXXII: 'Jaculum' read as 'baculum' (staff), and 'aero' as 'aereo' (bronze). LXXIV: 'liberarem' read as 'liberaretur'. LXXVII: 'iIlala diverborum' read as 'illata diversorum' (brought by various people). 'crux' is taken figuratively as a torment, and the clause is obscure.

The date "v Kalendas Junias" stands in parentheses in a displaced position in the printed text; it is taken here as the words the notary wrote. "post ejus Sanctus discessus" is read as "post, ejus sanctus discessus" (afterwards his holy departure). "peractum praelium" is taken as the struggle of his life. Several letters are garbled by scanning (cnbiculum, gloriOcandus); the evident readings are translated.

nodes.text: THE LIFE OF SAINT GERMANUS, BISHOP OF PARIS, BY VENANTIUS FORTUNATUS, BISHOP OF POITIERS. Carefully revised against the manuscript codices.

I. The blessed Germanus, then, bishop of the Parisians, a native of the territory of Autun, was born of honourable and respected parents, his father Eleutherius and his mother Eusebia. His mother, because she had conceived him in her womb within a short time after another [child], was moved by a woman's shame and wished to destroy the infant before birth: and having taken a potion to cast him out as an abortion, when it could do no harm, she lay pressing on her belly, to smother by weight the one whom poisons could not defile. The mother struggled with the little one, the infant resisted from the womb: there was thus a fight between the woman and her own inner parts. The matron was hurt, yet the infant was not harmed: the burden fought back, so that the mother should not become a murderer of her kin. It came about that, kept safe, he came forth unharmed himself, and rendered his mother innocent. From this one could foresee what was to come, that he had done a miracle before it befell him to be born.

II. Next, when as a boy he was going to school at the fort of Avallon with his kinsman Stratidius, Stratidius' mother, in order to acquire his inheritance, plotted the youth's death by deceit. She put a mixed potion in a little flask, and wine also in another, instructing a serving-girl that when the two came she should offer the one wine and the other the poison. But the servant, not knowing, switched the flasks and the cups; she gave the wine to Saint Germanus and the poison to Stratidius; and while destruction was being prepared for the innocent, the contriver fell into the snare. When his mother learned of this, she reproached the girl with weeping, [saying] that she had killed her son. As for Stratidius, though anxious care was spent on him and various remedies were made from those same poisons, although death did not take away his life, yet it left the mark of death fixed upon him.

III. From there, betaking himself to his kinsman Saint Scopilio at Lausia, he was raised and trained in honourable ways. Though they lived nearly a mile away from the village, they constantly ran to Matins, led by the warmth of faith through storm and through winter. Within the space of fifteen years he was made deacon by the blessed Agrippinus, and in the following three years he was ordained priest. Then by Bishop Nectarius he was taken on, being deservedly worthy, as abbot at Saint Symphorian's. With what abstinence he lived there, with how many vigils he persevered continuously, how lavish he was in almsgiving, one fact is witness: when all other goods had been given out to the poor, not even bread remained with which the brethren might be fed. Because of this, when the monks rose up against him, he shut himself in his cell, wept bitterly and grieved. Meanwhile, as he was praying, a certain matron Anna sent two pack-horse loads of bread. On the following day too she dispatched wagons full of grain: so that the monks, while they were sated with food, were awed by the miracle. So, intent and renowned in these duties, he did not cease to be made known by miracles worth proclaiming.

IV. Once, then, while he was taking food, weary, the monk Amandus went into the hayloft with a light; a coal fell, the flame caught the hay, and the greedy fire licked up the dry fuel. The others ran together, but did not rush in; he himself, leaping up somewhat later, snatched a pot from the hearth, climbed up onto the building singing Alleluia, and pouring a little water in the shape of a cross put out the blaze: and by a shower from the Saint's hand the wave of fire was quelled which rivers could scarcely have put out. On the next day the enemy himself, by whose snares it had been done, confessed it.

V. A certain Frank, Chariulf, had stubbornly seized part of the property of the basilica's estate. When the man of God warned him in some measure to return it, but did not succeed, he turned to prayer, and faith did not delay vengeance. At once a wild bear coming out from nearby killed three of his horses; even so he did not come to his senses from his hardness. On the following night the avenger doubled the ruin: it killed six beasts of burden, and even so the punishment was not enough. On the third night likewise it laid low nine draught animals, the carcasses tripled: thus the trouble grew into disaster. Then, belatedly, he sent a servant to the blessed man; he restored the seized land, and the calamity was checked. It came about that, with a beast chastising him, a man received sense, and a brute gave reason to one who lacked understanding.

VI. Next the blessed Agricola, bishop of Chalon, having a chamberlain gravely worn by the force of fevers, who, with mind made up, was wholly hanging on the point of passing, sent to the holy man for the help of his intercession. Then, having received the letter, he went to the basilica, beneath the portico, to the tomb of Saint Symphorian. Meanwhile the just man lay down in prayer, pressing the earth with his body and passing beyond the stars with his mind; and as though having the presence of the Lord before him, he came forward as petitioner for the suppliant's wish. For at once, being near the Redeemer's ears, he was heard, and while he was still lying in the dust, healing flooded the sick man; and while the just man lay on the pavement, the sick man rose from his bed, the cure running ahead before the one who begged had finished praying: so that the servant for whom a funeral was being prepared came out to meet the letter-bearer on his return; so that there was no doubt that the sick man was restored to health at the same hour at which the most blessed man was found to have prayed prostrate.

VII. Nor is it fitting to omit what was granted at the house of Ebro on account of the Just one's faith. As he entered the house, the matron Anna cried out that she saw a wonderful thing. Asked by her husband what it was that she was looking at, she said: 'See, blessed Germanus seems to me to be walking with a horned face: something I can scarcely bear either to look at with my eyes or to put into words, the holy man shining with horns in a new fashion.' And the woman, dismayed, marvelled that she could see a man in our own time in the likeness of Moses. It is to be believed that he too, after converse with the Lord, could be recognised by a woman as exalted with a horn. Out of fear at this, Ebro on that same day by no means dared to sit beside the Saint, for a twofold reason, grief and terror alike.

VIII. It happened that, on behalf of the estates of the church of Autun, he went to meet King Theudebert at Chalon. Mindful of Saint Symphorian at the entrance of the palace, he spoke with the Spirit of God so overflowing that the king assented before the petitioner had set out his words. And with prophetic mouth he told him the end of his passing. Within a few days after that, while he was returning to Reims, on the journey itself the king died by his final lot, as though the holy man's word had been spoken by an angel.

IX. And since it was the most blessed man's custom to keep vigils alone in the basilica of Saint Symphorian, as he was going the monk Sylvester followed him. And having entered together to the tomb of the holy martyr, around the middle of the night they heard noises of a crowding uproar from the altar, as if a multitude gathered for plunder were rushing in. The man of God, believing that an attack of robbers was under way, ordered the monk to sing psalms before the tomb. He himself went to the altar. Then that throng rushed eagerly to the monk where he was singing psalms. Having beaten him severely, thrown him to the ground and left him half-alive, they swiftly fled. He, scarcely able with tearful voice to recount his disaster, declared that he had been beaten by demons in a heavy assault.

X. It happened that a servant of Sabaricus, named Aesarius, having suffered injury, fled to the man of whom we speak, begging that at whatever price he would free him from the service of his insolent master. Sabaricus, indignant at this, demanded for Aesarius and his wife and his only son eighty solidi by way of price, or else he would not release the servants from servile subjection. Yet the Just one's mercy did not hesitate either to seek out or to give this. When the price had been paid, it happened that the oft-mentioned Sabaricus passed in front of the basilica, yet did not even come to prayer. Entering his house he was at once afflicted, bound, and, tied with chains, brought to the Saint. Not even so was mercy withheld by the pious man, but at once, prayer being offered, by his prevailing faith he was cleansed. Then Sabaricus added a further twenty gold pieces to the price he had received, and from the hundred solidi a cross was hung by him at the tomb of blessed Symphorian: which to this day stands as witness. On this occasion his sons and daughters lived so holy a life that they now rule bands of monks in monasteries. That affair in a wonderful way benefited the father and his offspring, so that the father's small wrongdoing passed to his descendants into mourning.

XI. This happened in the district of Alise. The wife of the illustrious man Vulfarius, named Destasia, bereft of the comforts of hope of life, lacking the use of her tongue, already mute for two days, lying with her breath failing, was already quivering lifeless, with the funeral made ready. Blessed bread having been sent to her by his priest, and put into the mouth of the as-good-as-dead woman, her teeth forced open, as soon as the liquid of the blessing entered the half-living woman's throat, at once the as-good-as-dead woman began to draw strength in her breaths, her eyes closed by death sought the light of day, so that after the pallor of the dead her face turned to a flush, until, to the amazement of all, she rose up restored to life, and the bystanders proclaimed the grace of the author of the gift. Every year she paid a tribute as the price of her life.

XII. For the rest, who could enter as an investigator of his revelations, from whom, four years in advance, the very matter of his episcopate was not hidden? So, while he was asleep, he saw keys of the gate of Paris being held out to him by a certain old man. Asking what this meant, he received the answer that he should keep them safe. Afterwards, when the bishop of that city died, as he went to meet the most excellent King Childebert, that voice earned its fulfilment in his election. And how he conducted himself, of what kind and how great, once ordained bishop, mortal tongue is not sufficient to set forth, since all that he did was beyond man. In short, having attained the rank of pastoral care, in other respects he remained a monk. On the one hand he exercised himself with frequent vigils, on the other he wore himself down with continual fasts. His chilled old age kept watch all night through the winter, bearing a twofold cold, of age and of season, which even wanton young men could not endure: almost forgetting himself for the victory over the body, as if dignity and necessity had come upon him together; and as for the alms which were made through the Saint's hands, whether from the property of the church or from the offerings of the people or from royal gifts, he alone who knows all things knows and counts them.

XIII. Then on one occasion, when the most excellent King Childebert had sent him six thousand solidi to be given out to the poor, he spent three thousand and returned to the palace; asked by the king whether there still remained anything to give to the needy, he answered that half remained, and that he had not found poor people on whom to spend it all. The king said to him: "Lord, give away what is left: for, with Christ granting it, what may be given will not run short": cutting up gilded dishes, breaking up silver vessels, giving whatever he had first to hand to the bishop so that he should not be at a loss. So there was a contest to be looked for between the bishop and the prince. They waged a battle of mercy with one another and a competition in kindness, to scatter treasures, and that the needy might grow rich from their talents, hastening towards future gains; that they might sow a seed of gold leaf and afterwards come as reapers through a golden crop: so that the bishop was enriched with royal treasures, and the bishop's favour flourished towards the king, who believed only that to be his own which the naked or needy had received.

XIV. But let us return to the sequence. A certain man in the village of Essonne, one of the servants of the fisc, named Gildomeris, having done some work on the Lord's day, was so cramped in his fingers that the points of his nails passed through to the other side. He came to the holy man at Paris in the oratory; and when a prayer had been said and his hand anointed with oil, the nails were drawn back out of the palm. Their function was restored to the fingers, and the web of the sinews was rewoven to its former service. Having made him a cleric after the cure, so that he might make him wholly safe, he freed him from both affliction and guilt.

XV. Again, a certain woman named Favonia in the city of Paris, taking nothing for nine days but a little gruel, gaping with her mouth open, was brought to the holy man. She, as if a piece of iron had been set between, could by no means bring her teeth or lips together. Anointing her with oil in the sacred oratory, and feeling her head all over, he restored her to health without delay.

XVI. It happened that a certain girl of the household of Medard of *Moglidonum*, spinning on the Lord's day, was punished with a cramped hand. When it was touched with oil, power poured in the remedy. Then the numbed fingers recovered their former vigour, the joints, restored, practised the forgotten work of their craft, the branching hand was stretched out, and the right hand, purged of its defect, was brought back to health.

XVII. It is rightly believed that this miracle too should be included. A certain Bobolinus from the village of Noyon, violently seized by the snares of the enemy, was brought bound in chains to the man of God; whirled about by the rebellious spirit, he was shaken and did not tire. He, while the holy man prayed, returned on the seventh day to himself and his own mind, as if from a long journey. Thus doubly freed, while the shadow fled from his senses, the chain fell from his hands, and he was returned both sound and unbound.

XVIII. And this must be handed down to memory by perpetual right. A certain man of the household of Nantharicus, the joints of his jaws separated from each other, was brought with his mouth open to the holy man. Having restored him to health by making the sign of the cross, he forbade him to take a drink of wine or food of meat. He, disregarding the command, was at once brought back to the condition of his illness. But so that the negligence of the transgressor should not take away glory from the just man, he was brought to him again at the estate of *Spedotenum*. Anointing the places of his jaws with holy oil, and pressing together his chin and lips with his blessed hands, calling on the name of Christ, the joint, struck by the holy fingers, went back into place, and by the merit of his faith he was brought home whole.

XIX. Likewise a smith named Ligerius, seized by the madness of a turbulent demon, had broken out into such bestial ferocity that, bound with chains on neck and hands, he was barely dragged into the presence of the blessed man. He was the more pitiable in that, while he suffered violence from the enemy, a second punishment was added to him through the chains. Yet the bishop ordered him to be kept with him; and, as God rested from his work on the seventh day, so too, when a week had passed, he was snatched from the demon by the work of God; and thus, freed from the enemy, he was granted to return home in safety.

XX. Waddo, an illustrious man, a sharer in the king's counsels, suffering a twofold bout of fever and chill, was presented before the eyes of the holy man to be cleansed. Meanwhile, at the usual hour, shaken by a very severe fever, he urgently demanded at least water to cool himself. When it was refused him, he grew insolent and insulted the holy bishop. But the man of God, content to gain the victory, having finished a prayer, giving him a drink of hot [water], restored the man to his former health, and treated the impending danger with such an antidote, curing fever with something hot.

XXI. Nor should this miracle of a similar kind be passed over. A servant of Queen Chrodosinda, named Ulfus, was very severely troubled by a periodic fever. Seeking the help of a cure, he went to the bishop. The man of God resolutely led him to the baptistery. But as the Saint prayed he began to be afflicted more severely, being on the point of release. Burning and feverish he asked for a little water, but it was refused. Roused most bitterly by the bitterness of gall, he threw his belt at the Saint's feet, crying: "You, lord, are killing me, when you ought to have healed me. But let this be known to you, that I die through you. My life will be required of you by the king or by my kinsmen." Meanwhile, from the heat, he rolled about on the floor of the baptistery. As the blessed man prayed he fell into sleep, and awakened after a little while from sleep, the sick man was restored by him to complete health. Asked by the bishop why he had spoken so insultingly to the bishop, he answered, only giving him thanks, and confessed that he remembered nothing of his words.

XXII. When the most excellent King Childebert had given the blessed man a horse fit for the saddle as a mount, he who had given it asked him to keep it for himself and not give it to anyone. Meanwhile the blessed man, at a captive's request, gave the horse as ransom, since with the bishop the voice of a poor man counted for more than that of the king. So he ordered him to sell it for fifteen solidi. As the poor man was leading it, a merchant met him and got the said horse for twelve gold pieces. Having bought it, the merchant took it to the stable. But since he had given less than the man of God had prescribed, the horse died in the night, so that the Saint's word should not go for nothing. Hence the next day the buyer, with oxen yoked, dragged the dead saddle-horse out of the stable, a dead mount. He, in reverse fashion, was led out tied with the halter not by the head but by the feet.

XXIII. It is worth handing down to memory how the priest of Christ was accustomed to triumph even over kings themselves. So when he had come to the glorious King Chlothar as usual, and yet he had not been announced to him while the holy man stood before the palace, having waited before the entrance without being presented, he returned home from there. The following night was spent in vigils in the oratory; the king was tormented by pain and an attack of fever. Scarcely at first dawn the nobles came running to the church house; the king's suffering was explained, and the great men begged that by his visit he would soften the force of the king's pain. At once, in his kindness, the matter of the insult was set aside; he who before had not even been announced entered the palace honoured and entreated. The king scarcely rose from his bed, and complained that he had been struck by a divine scourge. He licked the holy man's little cloak, and drew the bishop's garment over the places of pain. Having confessed the guilt of his offence, at once all pain was driven away: and it so came about that from him through contempt of whom he had incurred danger, he felt by touch the remedy.

XXIV. This happened at Vicus Novus in the district of Paris. A certain man in that same place, mangled by the attack of a rabid wolf and driven out of his senses, was pitiably brought to the blessed bishop. He, having recourse to those aids of his art, at once smeared the arm with the liquid of blessed oil and handled it healingly with his sacred fingers. That plague, which had pervaded his innards with spreading pain, fled the places it had besieged, and, the putrefaction now dissolved and his former vigour restored, without delay, as if he had woken from sleep, the pain withdrew and his mind returned.

XXV. Likewise from the village of Mantola, the maidservant of a certain Waldullus, struck with severe blindness for a year and nine months, was warned in sleep that if she touched the Saint's hem she would at once recover her sight. One day she came to meet the bishop; but she was wrapped in such deep night, her eyes so tightly closed, that they gave no opening through which he could put in the blessed oil. Nevertheless, having anointed the eyelids from above and the other parts of the head, and having said a prayer and signed bread and salt, he told the woman to withdraw to her lodging. He himself kept vigil in the oratory from first sleep; about the middle of the night the woman cried out that her guest was weeping profusely. Then, when a light was lit, she saw blood flowing from the joining of her eyes. When she came back to the Saint in the morning with this same blood, he bathed and washed the eyelids with water, adding prayers, and one eye was opened; then, the other having been anointed, the woman returned home. After this, during the same night, after a great flow of blood, as day approached she presented herself to the bishop. As he was returning home from meeting the king and entered the oratory, at once the woman's second eye was opened, and by the Lord's gift she rejoiced to see with twin light.

XXVI. The girl Magnofledis, when she was being mocked, deceived by such snares that whenever she wished to go to church she could not take a step, was presented to the servant of God at the estate of Savara. As soon as the Saint's hand was laid on the head of the staggering girl, by this searching the hidden guest was uncovered, and confessed with much groaning that it had long lain hidden, and cried out that in the presence of a Saint it could not conceal itself by its own trickery. So it complained in great burning that it was thus betrayed and must go out. Meanwhile, as the bishop did not cease to trace the sign of the cross with his hand, while all looked on, bursting out in the likeness of a fly, the enemy came out with blood from the woman's nostrils. When she had been restored to health, her dress changed for a monastic habit, and given over to the service of God, he made her triumph twice, over the enemy defeated and over the world.

XXVII. What of that, that he cured a crippled right hand without delay? When he had come to Tours for the feast of Saint Martin, as he came out of the monastery a barbarian woman presented herself, her hand contracted in its sinews, asking for healing. Taking it under his chasuble, he smeared it with his spittle and kneaded it as one kneads scattered flour gathered together. Then, as the right hand sweated, he stretched the fingers and bent them back, and roused the long-standing numbness to liveliness. And before he came to the door of blessed Martin he restored the right hand sound, its fingers extended. As soon as he felt it was straightened, he pushed the woman away from him and entered the basilica.

XXVIII. Then, as the servant of God came out of the said basilica and was going back to his lodging, another crippled woman presented herself, her palm fixed to her fingers; first touched with saliva, then anointed with oil, she was restored on the spot to her former health. For with the holy man, to cure the causes of infirmity was the same as to touch.

XXIX. It was truly marvellous: whenever the servant of God wished to go to Autun, the demons at once announced it at Saint Symphorian. And running to meet him through the Morvan, they cried out with weeping and groaning: "Holy man, if you drive us thoughtlessly from inhabited places, at least grant [us] to live in the solitude of the forests, so that we wretches may wander safe through the wildernesses. Before your eyes neither bodies nor woods hide us." Weeping and unable to bear the Saint's presence, when his right hand was applied they were put to flight everywhere from the bodies they possessed, and the demons, cast out, lamented over the people's salvation.

XXX. Let that noble miracle be brought forward. As the bishop was returning from Saint Symphorian, travelling on his way he entered the fortress of Avallon, where a multitude of accused men was held in prison. Then, invited to dinner by Count Nicasius, the man of God began to speak with him about mercy: that, sureties having been given, they should be released from their chains, and that he should remit part of the guilt out of regard for compassion. This he put off doing with obstinate spirit. So before he had finished dining, the Saint rushed from the table, and, standing above the underground prison, prayed at length with weeping, that by divine help might be granted what had not been obtained from the temporal judge. Thus that course of tears rose through the air to heaven, and the groaning reached its goal. And so an angel was appointed to bring it about. Then the venerable man, promising hope, encouraged those shut in. Nor did his speech lose what it said: faith was fulfilled in deeds. As he departed, at once the links of the chains were broken, the bound doors were unbarred, day was brought back into the prison, the condemned came out from darkness into light, and punishment no longer held those it would torment. Thus rescued, those who had been in peril shut up ran to meet the bishop at Paris. And so that he might grant something more to the guilty, he obtained from the king whatever was owed by them to the treasury.

XXXI. After this, when Nicasius wished to go to meet the holy man, and was already in his presence, at once he was thrown to the ground by a most grievous fall, and, when he had been left almost without any comfort of recovery, through the Saint's own intercession strength and sense returned to the despaired-of man. At once he handed over to blessed Germanus as a gift the belt with which he was girded and his sword: which he himself later redeemed by paying a price. It came about that what he had earlier put off granting to the prisoners, he as debtor made up for with doubled interest, and repaired the loss with an increased payment: first putting off [mercy] for them, afterwards redeeming even himself. Before not merciful to them, now fearful for himself too, he learned by his own mishap to succour the troubles of others.

XXXII. Indeed let that astonishing thing be retold on the page. As the holy man was going to visit the blessed martyr Symphorian, while he was proceeding from the village of Cervedo in the Morvan, the inhabitants of the place came to meet him and urged that he should see fit to visit the crop of Panitia, a widow woman who had nothing else left, which was being laid waste by bears, so that the attack might be driven off by his holy coming. He was led quickly to the place while his attendants laughed, and having said a prayer he made the sign [of the cross] over it. Then by divine prompting a savage rage was kindled in the related beasts, hatred was born in affection, battle was joined in peace. The beasts were armed with double fury; at once one bear was choked by the other, and the one that had survived, as it tried to get out, was run through by a stake of the hedge. Thus both ravagers were destroyed in one moment, and they themselves at once became weapons of death to each other. Afterwards, as he returned, the woman eagerly offered him the bears' skins, and presented the spoil as if to her victor; which, however, he utterly refused to accept; and those who had laughed before began to repent, seeing the miracle.

XXXIII. And since there should be no weariness over the gift of God, we think that too should be briefly set out. A certain woman, Beretrudis, a matron of Munsunthus, when at the time of the Litanies she could not go with the people because of her blinded eyes, hearing the choir of those singing psalms, implored with tears the help of lord Germanus. On the third night following, the most blessed man seemed to her in sleep to stand near her bed and to make the sign [of the cross] as if over her blind eyes. Waking, the woman told her husband what had happened. At once, as blood dripped, daylight was restored to her eyes, and after long cloud her eyes shone with a clear ray. And as the day grew bright the woman went forth in procession with the people to Mass, so that the image of the holy man, thus seen in a dream, was [her] remedy.

XXXIV. Here too is something no less praiseworthy: life restored to a little girl. When in the territory of Tours the wife of the illustrious man Pientius was lamenting the last moments of her daughter, who had been given up, and the little girl, her eyes closed, was not breathing with any stirring breath, she committed all her hope of help to the holy man's presence. He, invited by a messenger, hurried as fast as he could to the body of the girl already mourned as dead. Received with many tears by the weeping household, he approached the couch on which the little girl was already stiffening. He did violence to heaven with his pleas. When about the space of one hour had passed in this, with a stirring sob the girl's breath was brought back, and the vital heat of her innards spread through her limbs. Then, gradually reviving, she asked for a drink. Then, when she had tasted bread signed by the blessed man and the cup, all was turned to health for the little girl recalled from death. She later completed the course of a happier life in the monastery of blessed Radegund.

XXXV. A certain cleric from near the monastery of blessed Silvester in the territory of Tonnerre, having on a Sunday, as we say in common speech, "rounded" his boots, incurred a crippling of his hands and feet. But from blessed Silvester he recovered the use of walking; warned in sleep, he came to Saint Germanus, asking for the benefit of healing. Questioned by him, he confessed the cause, his fault. Then he ordered the cleric to proclaim among the people that no one should rashly work on Sunday. When the fifth day had passed, oil was poured over [it], the crippled hand was straightened, and he was sent off free to go to his own home.

XXXVI. Let what was done in the district of Amoniense be retold. At Rotegiacum, an estate of the church of Paris, seven raving men were brought to him. When they were cured, one who was possessed by a more grievous spirit, when he was forced to go out, declared to the man of God that, being expelled from that place, he would make grievous lamentation for the Parisians. Then the plague, put to flight, spread among the people a rumour of the passing of the holy man Germanus, and moved the flock to weeping over the death of its shepherd. Yet that possessed one, though he sowed a lie, being expelled did not keep hold of the one he had possessed.

XXXVII. And because the deeds of the Just One compelled the miracles to grow, again in the aforesaid place a paralytic was brought to him, his limbs loosened, carried in a cart, deprived of walking and of action. When the liquid of the sanctified oil had been poured over him and touched the surface of his skin, vigour entered his marrow. Then his revived hands returned to the use of movement; the chest, with the vital [breath] driven into it, became stronger; the weakness of the column-like knees was strengthened; the soles were set upright on firm bases. Meanwhile the whole structure of his limbs was restored. Having recovered his health, he met the holy man on the road as he was returning, with a gift prepared, giving thanks to Christ for his poor body restored.

XXXVIII. Nor should it be passed over how by like merit his power shone forth in another. Emmegesilus, then, from the village of Bucciacum, a boy still very small, paralysed in his limbs, was carried in a chair to Paris to the holy man by the hands of bearers. His right hand had no strength to move, his foot did not rise to stand firm, his tongue made no fluent sound; captive to the wasting of complete infirmity, he had been poured out, as it were, into the world of things without the order of nature. The saint anointed him continuously for three days with holy oil, restoring him to health in a single moment in voice, hand and step. Amazement seized everyone, and a cry was raised to heaven that Saint Germanus had surpassed all the art of physicians.

XXXIX. Likewise from the same village of Bucciacum a certain woman came to Paris with her hand so contracted that the points of her nails pierced into the inside of her palm. With only the saliva of his mouth drawn over her with his thumb, he restored the stretching of the sinews and the shape of the hand.

XL. The district of Bourges too keeps his laurels. When the good shepherd, with his customary concern for visiting the king, had come from the village of Novigeotum to Vicus Novus, a certain old woman presented herself who had spent twice four years in blindness. The bishop, placing the sign of our redemption over her eyes, ordered her to follow and go where the bishop went. On the next day, when she met him unexpectedly at the aforesaid [place], her eyes, with blood flowing from them in a plentiful stream, were weeping out her health. She was noticed among the others by the holy man standing there. Rising from his seat, he drew the woman, still blind as she was, into the lodging where his chamber was. Washing her eyes with warm water with his own hands, he poured daylight back into them. As soon as she saw the light, insatiable in her joy she put the holy man's fingers into her mouth, while the attendants, falling into compunction, said that they were seeing a man who in the house dispensed sight to the blind for money. But these things were done in the chamber in my presence.

XLI. When the bishop was approaching a property of the church called Inethe, a certain man came to meet him, complaining that he alone in a certain estate was well, while all the inhabitants were suffering from a grievous sickness. When his blessed bread had been carried to the sick, at once every weakness was put to flight from the ailing, and at the first taste of the blessed bread the disease was consumed along with the bread. So health was eaten with food by that crowd!

XLII. Again, when the man of God was going to the basilica of the blessed Cross at Paris, a woman laid before the saint a little child in white garments, gasping with its last breath and already about to depart, saying: "Kind father, if you would look upon one lamenting, I, a tearful mother, would not be bereaved. Nor would you wish to leave here one full of groaning and emptied of her fruit. And unless you hasten to help, you see the unhappy son snatched from the breast by wrenching death. Either restore him, or obtain that I be buried together with him. Forgive, shepherd, a wretched woman whom her grief makes bold." As she pleaded tearfully, as soon as the blessed man's right hand had made the sign of the cross over the dying child, the one who was already growing cold in death asked for his mother's milk, like one waking from sleep. Thus in a moment of time the son was taken from the jaws of death, the mother from grief. At this the crowd standing around was shaken with amazement, an uproar was raised on all sides, and they gave thanks to the Creator for the reward of the bishop's outstanding time, by whom diseases and deaths were continually commanded.

XLIII. Then, when he came to the village of Bradeia in the territory of Paris, after mass had been celebrated a paralysed woman was brought to him in the sacristy, carried in a chair; she bore the functions of all her limbs condemned, retaining no strength in foot or hand. At once, having trust in Him who granted him generous gifts, he anointed her with the blessing of the life-giving oil; at once the disease was driven out, healthy vigour flowed in, and with her innards revived she was reborn to health better than to birth, gaining more from the gift than she had received from her origin. So much so that afterwards she made a tunic for the saint with her own hands, as a tribute, as it were, for the healing she had gained.

XLIV. [Report] has handed down to memory something that is pleasing in his praise. Audegisilus, mayor of the royal palace, when he was grievously afflicted by a quartan fever, came to the blessed man, trusting in his kindness. The man of God assigned him to his own cell and ordered him to stay there shut in with one deacon. Then the attendant, anxious and fasting, fearfully pondered what he should do to cure the sick man. So he laid the feverish man in his bed, wrapped all round in the blanket of the servant of God. That same day, at the touch of the noble garment, as if by the rush of a river, the whole fire of the quartan fever was extinguished. And when [the saint] returned from his meal and the chamber was unlocked, he rose healthy from the bed, while the attendant rejoiced at the reward of his health, his fast then broken. Thus by the touch of the blessed man's garment he worked healing while absent.

XLV. Let us pursue the provision for the journey we have taken up. When the man of God was setting out for Poitiers to the blessed confessor Hilary, a certain Baudofeifa from Senecorbiacum, an estate, scarcely brought by two people, was presented to him; she was mute, lame and crippled in the hands. Her tongue was stiff and immobile, her breath fluttering; part of her was wholly of the grave, so that to the eyes of onlookers what was left was a corpse. When in mercy he made the sign of the holy cross over her, at once all vigour spread through her limbs, the flowing streams of her veins were roused, the feeble numbness of her sinews was shaken off, and the whole structure was renewed with natural motions to vital use. Then the plectrum of her tongue was loosed, the clenched balls of her fingers were stretched out, the bases of her feet were made firm, and for the saint to quicken the whole mass of her body was the same as to touch it. As the cure gained strength, on the third day she came to the city on her own feet to meet the saint, giving him thanks.

XLVI. It is thought worthwhile to insert also this proclamation of healing. As the blessed man was passing through the district of Vendôme, he turned aside to Hansido to stay the night; there the strength of his blessing prevailed so much that whoever faithfully took away straw from the bed on which the holy man had rested carried off a gift of healing, and from the seed of chaff reaped a harvest of medicine.

XLVII. Let the city of Nantes bear witness here to a noble deed. When the man of God came there and was received with very devout attendance, Tecla, the wife of Damianus, a man active in business, came to meet him, begging that either the shepherd himself or his envoys should visit her husband. Because access to him was difficult for [the saint], he sent a deacon with his chrismaria. He hurried to the man as he had been ordered and touched the sick man's body. The next day, after being entreated, the bishop himself went to the invalid, who was cruelly tormented under a double torturer, pressed on one side by illness, on the other by the wound of gout, a pitiable man. Then the bishop of the Most High anointed the sick man with blessed oil. At that moment the invalid at once, his hands straightened, with his step made firm after long weakness, leapt up.

XLVIII. But that the mystery might be doubled in one house, and the cure that had gone before in the father might reach the offspring, having a daughter named Maria, blind, deaf and mute, they brought her to him. They laid the living corpse before the saint's feet, saying: "Good shepherd, bestow what still remains of healing upon this sick girl. For we believe it has been reserved for you, so that you may have the praise of it, that the family restored may gain from the bishop what it lost in its offspring." Then his outstanding compassion was called forth to tears; at once the warrior turned to the weapons of his own warfare, and to win the victory the strong pleader offered prayers. Then the blessed man, rising from prayer, anointed the parts of her head with blessed oil, and in the name of the Trinity, the threefold weakness driven away, at once the passages of her ears and eyes were opened, and while all applauded the mute girl was made to speak. When this was done, the merchants of the city of Nantes, each for his own remedy, devoutly either offered or sent money, as each was able, to the holy man to be distributed to the poor.

XLIX. Leudegesilus, an illustrious man, according to what he himself declared, whenever anyone of the household of his house caught an attack of any fever or some chill, would wash those letters which the saint's hand had written in a signature, and by this remedy restored very many of his people to health.

L. Having touched briefly on these, let us go on with the rest. A certain Chusinus, while improperly tending a horse on a Sunday, put his hand into a wound, and his finger swelled. Then, as the inflammation spread, the whole part of his arm was loosened with putrefaction. When the saint was travelling through the Beauce, he obtained by pouring out prayers that he should turn aside to his house. At once the man of God bathed his arm with warm water; moreover, anointing it with blessed oil, the wonderful physician bound it with cabbage leaves laid on top. Thus the precious care quenched whatever ulcer was in it. Afterwards, healed by such a poultice, he came to meet the holy man, giving thanks.

LI. Likewise a servant of the church named Libanius, while thoughtlessly closing a hedge on a Sunday, had his hands contracted by an immediate punishment; under the scourge of the disease he hurried to the holy man at Paris. The saint, having drenched him with the liquid of blessed oil, or rather sprinkled him with the ointment of the sacrament, and adding a prayer, restored him to health.

LII. Let the miracles run on through brief accounts of individual cases. For Andulfus, a cleric of the church of Paris, while on the day of the Resurrection he was shaking nuts from a tree in his own vineyard, was struck with blindness because he had worked on the day of illumination, and remained with a darkened face for the space of a year. Then, brought to the bishop and anointed with the holy unction, he was given back to daylight again, and the bishop's clear light purged the cleric's cloud. So whatever the minister lost, the healing prelate recovered.

LIII. And since the kinds of miracles increase with time: when the blessed man was going to be presented to the king at the estate of Rotegiacum, a cleric troubled by a spirit of wickedness was brought to him. When the adversary was driven out, in the sight of the bystanders, it came out of the possessed man's head like a little bird, the shadow put to flight. While the others chased it as it flew about the house, the saint himself crushed it under his feet; and when it was pressed by his foot, the deceiver was suddenly turned into blood, so that the praise was doubled: it could not escape being trodden on, and by the evidence of its own fall the many-sided trickster became blood, guilty of blood.

LIV. Let the district of Exmes bring forward among our accounts what is its own, so that a matter of light may not be kept in darkness from posterity. When the most holy man had turned aside on his journey to the estate of Tasiliacum, a woman was brought to him who had a double affliction, old age on the one side, blindness on the other. She began to beg for health with trembling words. Moved by the supplication of the old and feeble woman, he first prayed and then poured oil over her; the lamps of her eyes gave back rays of light, and once the windows were granted, the darkness fled. When she had been given light, those standing by, giving glory to God through whom Christ works, proclaimed the merits of Saint Germanus.

LV. The diseases must be counted, so that the fountain of the physician may be proclaimed. Daningus, son of Ardulfus, was so swollen with dropsy in his head, his eyes and his whole insides, that his whole belly was like a wineskin, and, with his vital organs penetrated, the diseased skin was translucent from within like glass. Despaired of by the physicians, he fled to the blessed man for a remedy as his last resort. As soon as he was stripped of his clothes and anointed by the holy hands, the liquid of the dropsy shut within was consumed by liquid, and water was dried up by the pouring on of oil. So in a wonderful way neither did the fluid come out, nor was the sickness kept in, by a praiseworthy art by which fluid was dried by fluid.

LVI. Likewise, when he came to the basilica of the most blessed Gervasius and Protasius to keep vigil, a certain blind man pressed him, begging for mercy. The man of God ordered him to lie between the altar and the relics of the saints. When this had been done, at first dawn he at once made the sign of the cross over his eyes, and light shone forth. And the physician's whole labour applied the cure by the power of the cross.

LVII. A woman from the district of Exmes, asking the holy man for alms, by some chance did not deserve to receive anything. After this a British priest sought the blessing and relics of the aforesaid [saint] for the illness of the ruler of his country. Setting out on his journey, he took lodging on the estate where the aforesaid woman lived. Her husband urged her that she too, like the others, should go out to meet the relics of lord Germanus. She scorned this because the holy man had not given her alms. But at once, in the place where she stood, as if fixed to a stake, she could not move a step; and with her hands contracted she was carried to the saint's relics by her husband's hand. Meanwhile, repenting of what she had said, she was brought back to health through the pity of the kindly man, confessing that sudden danger had come upon her for her contempt of him.

LVIII. And since by his merit seeds of health were scattered through every place, it happened that the venerable Flameris, abbot of Chinon in the territory of Tours, had received a letter signed by the hand of blessed Germanus. When he was visiting at his bedside one of his monks who had been lying ill with fevers for two years, the sick man asked where the page had come from. The abbot answered that it had been sent to him by lord Germanus. He asked for it to be handed to him. As he wiped a letter of his signature with his tongue, health went down into his insides, and the ink's writing overcame all ointments. Hence it was proved, when the sick man recovered, that we may say in common speech that he had licked health from the saint's signature.

LIX. Then, when he came to the fort of Carnona, a crippled man thrust himself on him with a contracted hand, because he had done some work on a Sunday. He ordered him to come quickly after him to the estate of Cariacum. When he arrived, as he anointed his fingers with holy oil, suddenly the withered palm grew green again to match the other. Moisture running between the skin and the bones, which had been bound tight, loosened the joints. The joints, almost disjointed, were stretched out again into fingers; the long-standing dryness, suffused, flowered again into five; and at once, the sore closed up, the right hand was given back healthy and stretched out between the physician's hands.

LX. It happened that the holy man, returning from the territory of Nantes, honoured with his footsteps the house of Nunnichius, an illustrious man. The lady of the house faithfully snatched a thread from his garment and stored it in the oratory; and when she fell ill, after vigils had been solemnly celebrated in honour of the saint and mass said, she was cured on the spot. So the most blessed man not only healed with his hand what he touched, but, merely named, spread cures abroad.

LXI. Attila, an illustrious man and a domesticus of the royal court, fell in the bath and badly injured his arm, and his whole hand had putrefied from the shoulder. When a physician was brought in and wished to treat him, a vein of his insides burst, and almost all his life's blood poured out in a moment. It was reported to the bishop that the man was at the point of death. Driven by compassion, the old man hastened there. He found him laid out, overcome, with his eyes closed, without any hope, amid the tears of those lamenting. He barely opened his jaws with the handle of a little knife and, having first offered a prayer, put a little cold water into his mouth once, a second and a third time. Meanwhile, waiting to see what the outcome would be, he sat by the bed. When about an hour had passed, the lifeless man was shaken by a reviving sob, and called back by the gentle motion of breath, he was brought back. The passage of his throat was restored, his insides loosened as breath passed through; gradually recovering, he returned from death to life. Then, as if woken from sleep, he asked who had been at his head. He was told by those around him that lord Germanus was present. He asked that the saint's hand be graciously held out to him, and began to speak thus: "Lord, you have called me back as I was going on a long journey." And at once he offered a bag full of money and a belt of great weight, for him to give to the poor as the price of his life or in thanks.

LXII. As the holy man was travelling to Autun and arrived at Rotegiacum, he learned from Abbo that certain men had been thrust into prison. So he humbly appealed to the tribune for their release; but that hard man did not consent. Then, by a careful plan, saying that he was going to walk around the field, he ran devoutly to the prison. And there he lay prostrate to pray, and there in the night-time the chains were shaken off, the strong rigidity of the torture was reduced to fragments, the heavy bolt was smashed, the door-post was torn from its hinge, the deadly prison was opened, and the condemned returned to the air of life as if from the tomb. So it happened that they came in and met him at Rotegiacum in the morning; and the tribune, who had not granted the saint the release of the accused, was himself made the accused.

LXIII. So, always intent and anxious for the salvation of all, when he had come to Bourges for the ordination of Bishop Felix, at the bishop's preaching a certain Jew, Sigerius, received the sacrament of faith and was converted. He had a wife in Judaism named Mammona. When she would not admit even a mention of conversion, and, admonished by the blessed man's messengers, shrank away, the teacher himself set out after keeping a vigil. When she would not even look at the blessed man, after the office of Terce had been sung, the bishop graciously moved his hand to the woman's forehead, as a work of compassion. At once those standing around saw smoke coming out of the woman's nostrils with sparkling fire, so that it became clear to all that, until the lurking enemy was cast out, the woman had resisted her own salvation through the one who held her hostage. Then, relieved of the enemy's burden, breathing again, she confessed that she had never before been able to look at the blessed man's face. At her request and entreaty she was found worthy to be made a Christian with her own household, and, as if the head had submitted, many of the Jews were converted by her example.

LXIV. It is fitting to insert here how the wandering light of an eye was called back. When he was travelling to Autun for the ordination of Bishop Syagrius, among the other citizens the illustrious Florentinus was brought there to give consent, having a blemish in his eye that somewhat detracted from his good looks, so that he was not thought to be blooming in his face. Meanwhile, as praises were being acclaimed for the bishop, he was struck unexpectedly in that same eye by someone who did not know [him], and with it torn from its place, it began to hang over his cheek, his sight in doubt. He rushed after blessed Germanus at headlong speed with a cry, loudly lamenting many things, as calamity is wont to speak. Then by the hand of Saint Germanus the eye was put back in its place, and he was sent by him to blessed Symphorian. He persisted in vigils for him until the lost eye, with its former blemish cleansed, was by an added benefit given back more whole, and it returned better after the wound than it had been by nature at birth. This Florentinus was afterwards ordained bishop at Mâcon.

LXV. How great the power of his sign [of the cross] was, among other things this affair, which is set out next, stands as testimony. When he was returning from the basilica of Saint Martin to the holy church's estate at Severiacum, he came up on the road with a certain young man, Amantius, whom he found being led bound in iron by Jews. He asked what he had done. The boy answered truthfully that he was being led in chains because he refused to submit to the Jewish laws. Then the Jews pretended [they could not] open the iron chains with the key. When the holy man made the sign of the cross over them, the iron bolt was at once torn open.

LXVI. Likewise, when he was going at Paris to the basilica of Saints Gervasius and Protasius to pray, the doors were locked and entry was denied him. Then the keys were sent for, and when even they did not open [it], he unfastened the bolt simply by making the sign of the cross. Amazement seized their minds at the miracle before them, that what could not be opened with a key to lead the way was opened by [his] power. These venerable things too were done in my presence.

LXVII. And because no metal withstood the blessed man, since wood, stones and iron were loosed before him, it happened one day at Paris that he prayed at the door of the prison, and the next night a light appeared in the prison to those thrust inside. He was seen to urge them to dig so that they might get out. Telling one another that they had seen lord Germanus, each of them reported the signs. Finding a rib-bone of a beast, they dug, removed a stone, and came to meet the aforesaid friend of God at the church in the morning, as he was returning to rest. So the image of the bishop was a cause of deliverance for many, and, in the manner of blessed Peter, the very likeness of our bishop gave remedies.

LXVIII. After they had been snatched away, the tribune of the city began to rage against the soldiers, judging it to have been their negligence, which is to be credited to the glory of the most holy man. With the judge's anger turned on the guards, he handed over those who used to do the guarding to be kept in prison, and, taking away the keys, the judge became guard to the guards. Meanwhile the blessed man invited the tribune to dinner. And while they sat together at the same meal, those very men who had been sent [to prison] in fetters in place of the accused came to the holy man's table. Since the tribune, holding the keys in his hands, could scarcely believe what he saw of those released, recognising that he had guarded the prison just as the soldiers had, pardon was given in turn, and the fault passed into grace.

LXIX. Let Orléans contribute its noble praise of the man. As the holy man was going out of that city, he heard the voices of the condemned in the prison, where there was indeed an underground dungeon. Going up on top of it and lying prostrate, the friend of Christ prayed with tears. And through the power of his prayer, on the following night the prison was opened and they fled for refuge to the basilica of Saint Anianus. And thus the blessed bishop, though only passing by, left help behind him.

LXX. Let it not be tedious to hear what Christ grants to the faithful, while the power and the number of miracles grow together. So a certain Parisian came to the most holy man, whose eye had swollen up like a fist, so that, as was said, it was going to ruin after the injury. At his request the man of God smeared the eye with the saliva of his mouth, and restored healing and grace to its sight.
LXXI. A certain Moverla at Paris, who had a pustule on her arm and was tormented with pains, came to the blessed man and was cured by the same remedy, the touch of saliva.

LXXII. But if we were to go through each of the miracles that flourished through his deeds in his present life, these things once begun would be without end; there will be no limit on the page. For wherever the bishop's presence turned, no medicine was lacking for any kind of disease, and as many wounds of the sick as presented themselves, so many seeds of health did he pour out. For whether we recount the first of the bishop's deeds or the last, many ulcers were cured by the saliva of his mouth and the possessed were cleansed. Though the wickedness of the enemy came before him in secret, its fraudulent deceit at once revealed itself: and because they could not hide from the holy man's sight, nor endure his presence, they bewailed their burnings with terrible howling, flitting from place to place they laid bare their crimes as well, suspended in the air: often, even without being questioned, they confessed their names too. Often the demons ran of their own impulse to the holy man to be tormented. Wherever his attendant held the saint's staff, there the possessed person hung, bound as if by a bronze chain, and was held with foot fixed as if by nails.

LXXIII. And because the enemy's snares were often laid for the holy man, so that either his horse would stumble, or a branch of a tree would strike him, or the water of a valley or ice would cause danger, at once the possessed confessed who, how many and in what manner, the whole deed and their number. And when he set foot out of the house or the church, you would see a slaughter of demons before the gaze of so great a bishop and conqueror. They fell in crowds around the saint's footsteps, sprawled in various ways: some mute, others shouting; some rigid, others writhing. And as they recounted their own deeds as if before a judge, they did not escape torments. But how much is this praise to the saint's glory, when many stupendous things were done by him in a moment beyond telling?

LXXIV. Furthermore, how lavish he was in almsgiving cannot be set forth, not even if the voice of the whole people were joined into one. Often content with a chasuble or tunic, whatever was left over he used to clothe a naked pauper with, so that the needy man was warmed while the giver went cold. How great too was his outpouring for redeeming [captives] can in no way be set out, either by place or by number. The neighbouring peoples are witnesses to it, Spaniard, Irishman, Briton, Gascon, Saxon, Burgundian, since they ran together from all sides at the blessed man's name to be freed from the yoke of slavery. But when there was nothing at all at hand, he sat sad and anxious, sterner in face, and harsh in speech. Then, if perhaps someone invited him to dinner, he would press the guests or his own attendants to contribute together enough to free even one captive from slavery, and so the bishop's spirit would breathe a little from its grief. And if the Lord sent something from somewhere to be distributed by the saint's hands, foreseeing it at once in the spirit he used to say: 'Let us give thanks to the divine Clemency, for the means of redemption has drawn near.' At once, without any doubt, the result was proved before their eyes. When he had received it in his hands, the wrinkle of his brow smoothed, the old man bloomed in his face, walked with a brisker step, his tongue flowed more cheerfully: so that you would think that the man, in redeeming others, was himself to be freed from the chain of slavery.

LXXV. Who could worthily recount what power of words rolled from his mouth when he preached to the people, so that all learning was struck with amazement, and compunction arose in common among all ranks, and you would believe from the mouth of the speaker that the words were formed by an angel, as he spoke more than a man, transported in ecstasy of mind, when, with their stains scraped away, he made the hearts of the people breathe the fragrance of divine spices through the purity of his teaching.

LXXVI. Riding on a journey, he always offered something to God, either in speech or in song, saying the office bareheaded even if snow or rain pressed upon him. And when he came to table, at once an attendant was there reading the divine discourses, so that amid the courses of food the guest might be more filled by the nourishment of the soul. He let no time intervene in which he did not either benefit others or himself make progress.

LXXVII. Who could relate what care he always spent on vigils? Or proclaim the cold he endured through the ardour of his faith? For often in his bed, before he roused the others from sleep to rise, he would sing fifty psalms or more, untiring, to the Lord in the temple of his heart. But who could have perceived by hearing or caught by sight that happy theft, when he often went from his bed to the oratory without shoes, so as not to be noticed by anyone, taking no witness to that theft except Christ? After celebrating the vigil, returning to his bed as if he had done nothing, he would only then wake the others. And what constancy he had in psalm-singing, when his flesh held out as if clad in the rigidity of iron, while the cold crusted the stones and turned the waters into a crust? Fighting with his own body and conquering, almost forgetting himself, so that, the domestic torment of the body overcome, he won a triumph over himself, made a martyr in peace: so that, while the clergy took turns, he himself, without relief, did not stop singing the chants. Indeed what follows is told as almost incredible: that entering the church at the third hour of the night, he did not leave the ranks of the singers again until, as the day grew bright, the whole office, solemnly sung, was completed according to the rule. And when he returned home, wearied by age or cold, either the petitions brought by various people disturbed him, or he was asked where he might give help: so that even when he lay down to rest, a cross was prepared for him in his bed, at least a little, from the complaints of the afflicted or the poor who came to him; he put aside his own discomforts, lest the need brought to him should weigh on the petitioner. Ready for mercy, always running to obtain pardon, father and shepherd of the people, taking others' cases and complaints upon himself, he either eased them in part, sharing their sorrows, or, as far as he could, remedied them entirely, helping with his whole heart.

LXXVIII. He was also so greatly enlarged by holy advancement that he even foretold the day of his blessed passing, as we set down here. Some days before, he called his notary to him and ordered him to write in his bedchamber, above his bed, only this: "the fifth day before the Kalends of June" [28 May]; but no one knew what this meant. After his death, his holy departure from the world made it plain; for the Lord did not allow this to be hidden from a soul so close to him. And so on that very day, after the battle was ended, the blessed man passed to Christ. Busy with these and similar pursuits, and always intent on them, being almost eighty, through deeds to be marvelled at throughout the world, to be joined to the martyrs, gathered to the apostles, glorified for his merits, crowned among the peoples, snatched from the bonds of the body, to live forever with a spotless spirit in the blessed endowments of faith, he flew up to heaven a victor, in the reign of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be glory, honour and power for ever and ever. Amen.
